newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks end lower; brace for key economic data.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks end lower; brace for key economic data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks changed course and ended lower Monday as investors braced for an onslaught of economic numbers, starting with a closely watched gauge of wage-fed inflation, the Employment Cost Index, on Tuesday.

"Some investors are locking in profits ahead of several important economic indicators due to be released later this week," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended 34.29 points lower at 5,972.73, after being up more than 35 points early in the day. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,530 to 865 on moderate volume of 383 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Private economists expect the third quarter Employment Cost Index to rise a moderate 0.8 percent -- the same pace as in the previous two quarters -- and not show a pickup in inflation that would spur the Federal Reserve to boost interest rates.
The market also will focus on the third-quarter gross domestic product data due on Wednesday and October jobless rate on Friday.

Analysts said the market's retreat stemmed from Wall Street concerns that the Democrats will retake the House of Representatives in the election and to tax-loss related selling by mutual funds in the final week of the month.

"There's nothing fundamentally wrong with the market. But there's the same worry that the Democrats will take Congress in addition to the presidency and that causes consternation among fund managers," said Thom Brown, a managing director at Rutherford Brown & Catherwood.
He said individual investors would likely complete their tax-loss selling in November. "It's going to mitigate against seeing the market go a lot higher."
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. said, "The market is shifting its attention to the economy and interest rates, a combination that will dominate this week."
With the bulk of third-quarter corporate earnings out, most of the good news is out of the market.

"It was a good showing but there were warnings (from corporations) that things are not getting better short-term," said Michael Metz, Oppenheimer & Co.'s chief investment strategist. "They told of (negative) currency translations and margin pressures."

Among individual shares, Loctite soared 12-1/8 to 58-1/8 after Germany-based Henkel said it intends to buy the remaining shares of Loctite that it does not already control for $56 per share, or $1.12 billion. Loctite, a maker of engineering adhesives, said it will review the proposal from its largest shareholder.

RJR Nabisco rose 7/8 to 28-7/8 after the company reiterated that it saw no spin off of its food unit prior to 1997. Oppenheimer & Co. said it saw an upside target of $35 for RJR if there is no spin-off and $40-plus if there is a spin-off.
Electronic Data Systems resumed last week's slide after warning of slower growth in the fourth quarter. EDS was the most-active NYSE issues and lost 5 to 41-1/8.
Physician Alliance plunged 4-5/8 to 4-7/8 on disappointing earnings and Transition Systems lost 5 to 8-3/4 after issuing an earnings warning.
In other merger news, Mercantile Bancorp, off 2-3/8 to 49-3/4, and Mark Twain Bancshares, up 3-5/8 to 46, agreed to merge in an $855 million tax-free exchange.
Revco rose 3/8 to 29-3/4 after agreeing to buy Big B Inc. for $17.25 a share, or $380 million. Big B rose 9/16 to 17-1/8.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 6.71 points to 1,215.89.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 3.66 to 697.26. The American Stock Exchange index lost 3.24 to 566.55.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 2.28 to 370.98. The average share was down 24 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,792.591 down 41.720 or 0.61 percent.
